text: The training loop.
Five steps, two thousand times.
Every lesson so far has a piece of training in it.
Tonight they go round together, and we watch the whole loop teach the attention model, from the first step to the last.
One lap goes like this.
Take a batch of 16 rows from the training text.
Run the model forward and score every next word: that is the loss.
Run backward to get the slope for every one of the model's 20,864 numbers.
Then the optimiser takes one step downhill.
That is one lap.
On one core of our test machine, with this lesson's own code, a lap takes about 21 milliseconds, and most of that is the backward pass: 14 of them.
The optimiser is Adam, with a little weight decay that shrinks most of the numbers slightly each step, as in AdamW.
The layer norms' gains and the biases are left out.
The step size starts tiny and grows over the first 30 laps to 0.01.
That is warmup.
And if the whole slope, all the numbers taken together, is ever longer than 1, it is shortened to 1 before the step.
That is clipping.
It fired on 76 of the 2,000 laps, 62 of them in the first 250.
Now run it.
At lap zero, the held-out loss is 3.84, a blind guess.
By lap 100 it is 0.97: the easy patterns, which word tends to follow which, come first.
Will copying a word from far back be learned early, late, or bit by bit?
Copying a word from far back comes late, and then fast.
At lap 500, copying is right 43 percent of the time.
By lap 750, 97 percent.
We ran the loop again from the same seeds, and got the attention lesson's model back exactly: 29 of 29 weight tables, number for number.
Change one setting at a time, train for 1,000 laps, and compare.

Ten times larger ends worse, at 0.95, copying 22 percent.
